summary: Once-daily MAO-B inhibitor used with carbidopa/levodopa for Parkinson “off” episodes. Not a psychiatric medication, but it can affect sleep, anxiety, impulse control, and hallucinations—and it has serious interactions with many antidepressants and other serotonergic drugs.
description: Safinamide is an add-on medication for Parkinson disease when carbidopa/levodopa wears off and symptoms break through (“off” time). It boosts dopamine signaling by selectively blocking MAO-B at recommended doses (≤100 mg/day). From a psychiatry lens, the big deal is safety: it can worsen insomnia or anxiety in some people, cause daytime sleepiness (including sudden sleep episodes), trigger impulse-control problems, and worsen hallucinations/psychosis. It also has major interaction landmines with many antidepressants, dextromethorphan, stimulants, and certain opioids—so med lists matter.
patient_summary: Safinamide is a once-daily add-on for Parkinson “off” episodes with carbidopa/levodopa. It’s not used to treat anxiety or depression—but it can affect sleep, anxiety, impulses, and hallucinations, and it has serious interactions with many antidepressants and other serotonergic meds. Don’t mix it with restricted medications (like certain antidepressants, dextromethorphan, stimulants, tramadol/meperidine/methadone, or other MAO inhibitors). Report new insomnia, agitation, compulsive behaviors, or hallucinations right away.

primary.condition_name: Parkinson disease (adjunct to carbidopa/levodopa for “off” episodes)

secondary.context: Adjunctive treatment to carbidopa/levodopa in people with Parkinson disease who experience “off” episodes. Not a primary psychiatric indication, but psychiatric symptoms (insomnia, anxiety, hallucinations, impulse-control problems) can meaningfully change tolerability and safety.
Insomnia has been reported as an adverse effect. If sleep gets worse after starting or increasing the dose, that’s clinically relevant and may require medication reassessment.
Anxiety has been reported as an adverse effect. New or worsening anxiety should be taken seriously—especially if it looks like activation, agitation, or mixed symptoms.

May exacerbate hallucinations or psychotic behavior, particularly in people with an underlying psychotic disorder or Parkinson-related psychosis. Consider dose reduction or discontinuation if psychosis emerges.

Impulse-control problems (compulsive gambling, spending, hypersexuality, binge eating) can occur in Parkinson therapy contexts. If these show up, dose reduction or discontinuation may help in some cases.

common_adverse_effects.notes: This medication can increase involuntary movements or make existing dyskinesia louder. Sometimes the fix is adjusting levodopa or other dopaminergic meds rather than abandoning treatment completely.
Usually manageable, but if nausea is persistent or severe, it can wreck adherence and quality of life—worth addressing early.
If your sleep gets lighter, shorter, or more fragmented, don’t just “push through.” Sleep loss can worsen anxiety, mood, and cognition—and can destabilize Parkinson symptoms too.
New anxiety after starting or increasing the dose can happen. It may feel like internal restlessness, activation, or irritability. Call it out early so the regimen can be adjusted.
Blood pressure can climb. This matters even more if anxiety symptoms overlap with physical signs like palpitations or headaches—check BP rather than guessing.
Dizziness when standing can look like anxiety or ‘panic-y’ symptoms. Hydration, slow position changes, and medication review are key.
Falls are a safety emergency in slow motion. If you’re more sedated, dizzy, or unsteady, your prescriber needs to know.

serious_risks.risk: Sudden onset of sleep / severe daytime somnolence: May fall asleep during daily activities (including driving) without warning; discontinue or restrict high-risk activities if this occurs.

Serotonin syndrome: Agitation, confusion, hallucinations, sweating, tremor/rigidity, diarrhea, fever, blood pressure instability, seizures—medical emergency; stop interacting agents and seek urgent care.
Hypertensive crisis (especially with nonselective MAO effects or very high tyramine intake): Severe headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, very high BP—medical emergency.
Impulse control disorder: Compulsive gambling, spending, binge eating, hypersexuality, other intense urges; can cause major psychosocial harm.
Psychosis/hallucinations: Can worsen hallucinations or psychotic behavior; urgent prescriber contact recommended.
Hypersensitivity reaction: Swelling of tongue/oral mucosa, dyspnea—emergency care.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to safinamide or any component of the formulation (eg, swelling of tongue/oral mucosa, dyspnea)
Concomitant use of or use within 2 weeks of other MAO inhibitors or potent MAO inhibitors (including linezolid)
Concomitant use with or within 2 weeks of SNRIs, TCAs, tetracyclic antidepressants, or triazolopyridine antidepressants
Concomitant use with methylphenidate, amphetamine, or their derivatives
Concomitant use with certain opioids (eg, meperidine, methadone, propoxyphene, tramadol)
Concomitant use with St John’s wort
Canadian labeling (additional): Albinism, retinal degeneration, uveitis, inherited retinopathy, or any active retinopathy (including severe progressive diabetic retinopathy)

precautions: CNS depression and sudden sleep episodes: Can cause significant daytime sleepiness and falling asleep during activities (including driving) without warning
Hypertension risk: Can cause or worsen hypertension; doses above 100 mg/day reduce MAO-B selectivity and increase hypertension risk
Serotonin syndrome: Potentially life-threatening when combined with serotonergic agents or other MAO inhibitors
Impulse-control problems: Compulsive gambling, spending, hypersexuality, binge eating, and other intense urges can occur
Psychosis risk: May worsen hallucinations or psychotic behavior—especially in those with a psychiatric vulnerability
Dyskinesia: May cause or worsen dyskinesia, often improved by adjusting dopaminergic therapy
Hepatic impairment: Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C); max 50 mg/day in moderate impairment (Child-Pugh B)
Tyramine caution: At ≤100 mg/day, tyramine reaction is unlikely, but very high-tyramine foods/drinks can still trigger hypertensive crisis
Ophthalmic caution: Use caution in patients with retinal/macular disease or inherited retinal conditions; monitor for visual changes

interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated due to risk of serotonin syndrome and hypertensive reactions with MAO-related mechanisms.
interactions.action: Avoid coadministration and avoid starting within 2 weeks of each other unless a specialist explicitly manages a transition plan.

interactions.interactant: Other MAO inhibitors or potent MAO inhibitors (including linezolid; other MAO inhibitors intended for psychiatric use)
interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated. Increased risk of severe reactions including hypertensive crisis and serotonin syndrome.
interactions.action: Do not combine. Maintain appropriate washout periods (commonly 2 weeks) based on the interacting agent.

interactions.interactant: Serotonergic agents (SSRIs, triptans, fentanyl, lithium, tramadol, buspirone, tryptophan, St John’s wort)
interactions.action: Avoid where contraindicated; otherwise, use only with careful risk assessment, lowest-risk alternatives, and close monitoring for agitation, confusion, autonomic instability, tremor/rigidity, and GI symptoms.

interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated. Can precipitate serious CNS toxicity and serotonin syndrome-like reactions.
interactions.action: Avoid all OTC cough/cold products that contain dextromethorphan. Read labels—this one is sneaky.

interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated. Increased risk of hypertensive crisis and severe reactions.
interactions.action: Do not co-prescribe. If ADHD treatment is needed, coordinate care and consider non-stimulant strategies with specialist oversight.

interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated. Risk includes serotonin syndrome and severe toxicity.
interactions.action: Avoid. If pain management is needed, coordinate with prescriber/pharmacist for safer alternatives.

interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated due to MAO-related interaction risk.
interactions.action: Avoid; use alternative muscle relaxants only with careful review.

interactions.mechanism: At ≤100 mg/day, tyramine interaction is unlikely, but very high tyramine intake can still trigger hypertensive crisis.
interactions.action: Avoid foods/beverages with very high tyramine (>150 mg) and avoid spoiled/improperly stored foods.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Blood pressure: Baseline, periodically, and as clinically indicated (watch for new or worsening hypertension).
Daytime sleepiness: Ask directly about drowsiness, nodding off, and any sudden sleep episodes—especially if the person drives.
Falls risk: Screen for dizziness on standing, unsteadiness, sedation, and new falls; reassess driving and home safety if risk increases.
Psychiatric status: Monitor for new anxiety, agitation, insomnia, hallucinations, paranoia, or psychotic behavior—especially after starting or dose increases.

Impulse-control behaviors: Ask about gambling, shopping/spending, hypersexuality, binge eating, and other compulsive urges; involve family/caregivers when appropriate because people often under-report.
Hepatic function: Baseline and as clinically indicated; dosing limits apply in moderate impairment and severe impairment is contraindicated.

Vision monitoring (high-risk patients): Periodic checks for visual changes in those with retinal/macular degeneration, uveitis, inherited retinal conditions, albinism, retinitis pigmentosa, active retinopathy, or family history of hereditary retinal disease.
Medication interaction surveillance: Reconcile all prescriptions, OTC products (especially cough/cold meds), and supplements at every visit; ensure washout periods where relevant.

special_populations.pregnancy: Adverse events were observed in animal reproduction studies. Parkinson disease in pregnancy is relatively rare, and when treatment is needed, agents other than safinamide may be preferred. If safinamide is considered, decisions should be individualized with neurology and obstetrics involvement, weighing maternal function and fetal risk.
special_populations.lactation: It is not known whether safinamide is present in breast milk. The manufacturer recommends weighing the risk of infant exposure against the benefits of breastfeeding and the benefits of treatment to the mother. If used, monitor the infant for sedation, feeding issues, and unusual irritability, and coordinate with pediatrics.
special_populations.geriatric: Refer to adult dosing. Older adults may be more vulnerable to falls, orthostatic symptoms, and CNS depression; start at recommended dosing and monitor closely for sedation, sudden sleep episodes, and blood pressure changes.
special_populations.renal_impairment: No manufacturer-recommended adjustment. Dose adjustment is unlikely to be needed given limited unchanged urinary excretion; monitor clinically as part of overall medication safety.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Mild impairment (Child-Pugh A): No dose adjustment necessary. Moderate impairment (Child-Pugh B): Maximum 50 mg once daily. Severe impairment (Child-Pugh C): Contraindicated (not studied; manufacturer contraindication).

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Predominantly metabolized to inactive metabolites by non-microsomal enzymes (cytosolic amidases/MAO-A); CYP3A4 plays a minor role
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Can be taken without regard to meals; at doses ≤100 mg/day, tyramine interaction is unlikely but very high-tyramine intake can still pose risk

dosing.titration: Safinamide is taken once daily and must be used with carbidopa/levodopa. Typical start is 50 mg daily; after 2 weeks, some people increase to 100 mg daily if needed and tolerated. If stopping, step down to 50 mg for one week before discontinuing.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Safinamide isn’t a benzodiazepine and doesn’t have a classic “benzo withdrawal” profile, but abrupt changes in Parkinson regimens can still cause serious problems. The practical rule: don’t stop suddenly unless you’re told to for safety. If you’re discontinuing, step down first.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Safinamide (Xadago/Onstryv) is an add-on medication for Parkinson disease when carbidopa/levodopa isn’t holding all day and you get “off” episodes. It’s not prescribed to treat anxiety, depression, or insomnia—but it can absolutely affect those symptoms (for better or worse) because it changes dopamine signaling and comes with MAO-related interaction rules.
items: {link:condition:parkinson-disease:Parkinson disease}: Adjunct to carbidopa/levodopa for patients experiencing “off” episodes (wearing-off periods)

Medication-safety planning: Often chosen or avoided based on psychiatric side effects (sleepiness, insomnia, anxiety, hallucinations, impulse-control issues) and interaction risk with antidepressants/serotonergic meds

quotes: My brain felt more ‘on’ at night, and sleep got lighter.
I could fall asleep, but I’d wake up more.
It helped my movement, but my sleep took a hit.
items.note: Insomnia can show up even when the medication is helping Parkinson symptoms.

quotes: I felt more keyed up—like my body had caffeine in it.
My anxiety crept up after the dose increase.
It wasn’t panic, just this wired, uneasy feeling.
items.note: New or worsening anxiety after starting or increasing the dose should be flagged.

quotes: I started shopping like it was a hobby I couldn’t quit.
My urges felt stronger and harder to ignore.
It was like my ‘pause button’ got weaker.
items.note: Impulse-control problems can happen in Parkinson treatment contexts; they’re not a character flaw.

quotes: I felt paranoid in a way that wasn’t normal for me.

items.note: If hallucinations or psychotic behavior appear, this is an urgent prescriber conversation.

sections.intro: This isn’t a “psychiatric med,” but people still notice brain-and-behavior changes. These are the patterns that matter most in real life:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Safinamide is taken once daily. It reaches peak levels a few hours after a dose, and it sticks around long enough to feel “steady” day-to-day rather than spiking and crashing.
key_points: 2-3 hours: Time to peak levels after a dose
20-26 hours: Half-life (slow enough for once-daily dosing)
Daily dosing: Effects build into a consistent baseline rather than an immediate “take it and feel it in 30 minutes” effect

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Safinamide’s main job is Parkinson symptom control as an add-on to carbidopa/levodopa. From a psychiatry viewpoint, the “efficacy” story is mostly about what it does to sleep, anxiety, impulse control, and hallucinations—because those effects often decide whether someone can stay on it safely.
sections.clinical_details: If someone becomes more anxious, can’t sleep, starts having compulsive behaviors, or develops hallucinations after starting or increasing safinamide, that’s a clinically meaningful outcome even if motor symptoms improve. The intervention is usually dose adjustment, medication review for interactions, and reassessing overall Parkinson regimen (and sometimes stopping safinamide).

patient_counseling: Tell your prescriber every medication and supplement you take—especially antidepressants, cough meds (dextromethorphan), stimulants, certain opioids, triptans, and St John’s wort.
If you feel sleepy in the daytime or ever “nod off” without warning, do not drive. This is a stop-and-call situation.
Watch for new insomnia, agitation, anxiety, or a wired/restless feeling after starting or dose changes.
If you notice compulsive urges (gambling, shopping, sex, binge eating), say it out loud early—dose changes can help.
If hallucinations, paranoia, or confusion appear, contact your prescriber promptly—this can become dangerous fast.
Avoid very high-tyramine foods and spoiled/poorly stored foods; if you get a severe headache with high blood pressure symptoms, seek emergency care.
Do not stop abruptly. If discontinuing, your prescriber may step you down first.

sections.intro: Safinamide is an MAO-B inhibitor, and that comes with serious interaction rules—especially around serotonergic medications, stimulants, dextromethorphan, and certain opioids. When in doubt, don’t guess—verify.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Safinamide isn’t a benzodiazepine and doesn’t have a classic “benzo withdrawal” profile, but abrupt changes in Parkinson regimens can still cause serious problems. The practical rule: don’t stop suddenly unless you’re told to for safety. If you’re discontinuing, step down first.
key_points: Discontinuation plan: Decrease to 50 mg once daily for one week before stopping.

Why we avoid abrupt stopping: Sudden interruption of antiparkinsonian therapy can contribute to a discontinuation syndrome that can resemble neuroleptic malignant syndrome (high fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability).

If severe sleepiness, sudden sleep episodes, serotonin syndrome symptoms, or hypertensive crisis occurs: Stop interacting agents and seek urgent medical guidance immediately; emergency care may be required depending on symptoms.
If hallucinations/psychosis or impulse-control behaviors emerge: Dose reduction or discontinuation may help; coordinate with the prescriber rather than white-knuckling it.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Safinamide is taken once daily and must be used with carbidopa/levodopa. Typical start is 50 mg daily; after 2 weeks, some people increase to 100 mg daily if needed and tolerated. If stopping, step down to 50 mg for one week before discontinuing.

adult.adjunct_off_episodes_initial: 50 mg PO once daily (always in combination with carbidopa/levodopa)
adult.adjunct_off_episodes_titration: After 2 weeks, may increase to 100 mg PO once daily based on response and tolerability
adult.discontinuation: If discontinuing: reduce to 50 mg PO once daily for 1 week, then stop
adult.hepatic_limit_child_pugh_b: Moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B): maximum 50 mg PO once daily

sections.simple_explanation: This is a once-daily add-on to levodopa to help smooth out “off” episodes. It’s not about quick-onset calming like a sedative; it’s about steadier dopamine signaling—while carefully avoiding high-risk medication combinations.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Data in pregnancy and breastfeeding are limited. When Parkinson treatment is needed during pregnancy, other agents may be preferred. Hepatic status matters a lot for safinamide dosing and safety.

If safinamide is considered, decisions should be individualized with neurology and obstetrics involvement, weighing maternal function and fetal risk.

If used, monitor the infant for sedation, feeding issues, and unusual irritability, and coordinate with pediatrics.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Safinamide is available as an oral tablet taken once daily. Use it at the same time each day and always with carbidopa/levodopa.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Safinamide selectively inhibits MAO-B at recommended doses (≤100 mg/day). MAO-B is one of the enzymes that breaks down dopamine in the brain. By slowing dopamine breakdown, safinamide increases dopamine availability and supports dopaminergic activity. The exact way it improves Parkinson symptoms isn’t fully pinned down, but the dopamine effect is the core idea.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Safinamide lives in the Parkinson toolbox, not the psychiatry toolbox. But psychiatry shows up anyway—because the side effects and interactions are very “mental health adjacent.” If someone is on antidepressants, serotonergic meds, certain pain meds, cough products with dextromethorphan, or stimulants, safinamide may be a nonstarter. And if someone develops insomnia, anxiety, hallucinations, or compulsive behaviors, that can outweigh motor benefits and force a medication rethink.

faqs.q: Is safinamide used to treat anxiety or depression?
faqs.a: No. Safinamide is for Parkinson disease as an add-on to carbidopa/levodopa for “off” episodes. Psychiatry still matters because safinamide can worsen insomnia or anxiety in some people, and it can interact dangerously with many antidepressants and serotonergic medications.

faqs.q: Why are the interaction rules such a big deal?
faqs.a: Because safinamide is an MAO-B inhibitor. Mixing MAO mechanisms with certain antidepressants, dextromethorphan, stimulants, or specific opioids can trigger serious reactions—especially serotonin syndrome or dangerous blood pressure spikes. This is one of those meds where the medication list is the safety plan.

faqs.q: Can safinamide make you sleepy during the day?
faqs.a: Yes. CNS depression, daytime sleepiness, and even sudden sleep episodes have been reported. If you feel unusually drowsy, or you ever “nod off” without warning, do not drive—and contact your prescriber right away.

It can. Insomnia has been reported. If your sleep gets lighter, shorter, or more fragmented after starting or increasing the dose, tell your prescriber—sleep disruption can worsen anxiety, mood, and cognition, and it can destabilize Parkinson symptoms too.

faqs.q: What psychiatric symptoms should I watch for?
faqs.a: The big ones: new or worsening anxiety, agitation, insomnia, hallucinations, paranoia, confusion, and impulse-control problems (compulsive gambling, shopping/spending, hypersexuality, binge eating). If any of these show up, don’t wait—early dose adjustments can prevent a lot of damage.

faqs.q: What is serotonin syndrome and what does it feel like?
faqs.a: Serotonin syndrome is a potentially life-threatening reaction that can happen when serotonergic drugs are combined in unsafe ways (including MAO-related interactions). Warning signs include agitation or confusion, sweating, fever, fast heart rate, blood pressure swings, tremor, muscle stiffness, diarrhea, and sometimes seizures. If you suspect it, seek urgent medical care.

faqs.q: Do I need to avoid tyramine foods?
faqs.a: At recommended doses (≤100 mg/day), tyramine interactions are unlikely—but very high-tyramine foods and spoiled/improperly stored foods can still pose risk. The practical move is avoiding foods/beverages that are very high in tyramine and being careful with freshness.

Typical adult dosing is 50 mg by mouth once daily with carbidopa/levodopa. After 2 weeks, some people increase to 100 mg once daily if needed and tolerated. In moderate liver impairment (Child-Pugh B), the maximum is 50 mg daily.

faqs.q: How do you stop safinamide safely?
faqs.a: If discontinuing, the dosing guidance is to reduce to 50 mg once daily for one week before stopping. Don’t stop abruptly unless your prescriber tells you to for safety—sudden changes in Parkinson regimens can trigger serious symptoms.

faqs.q: Is safinamide safe if I have hallucinations or a psychotic disorder?
faqs.a: Use caution. Safinamide may worsen hallucinations or psychotic behavior. If hallucinations, paranoia, or confusion appear or worsen after starting or increasing the dose, contact your prescriber promptly—this often requires a medication adjustment.

Impulse-control problems have been reported in Parkinson treatment contexts, including intense urges like gambling, spending, hypersexuality, and binge eating. If this happens, it’s a medical side effect—not a moral failing—and dose reduction or discontinuation may help.

seo.description: Safinamide (Xadago/Onstryv) is a once-daily MAO-B inhibitor used with carbidopa/levodopa for Parkinson “off” episodes. Learn key interactions (antidepressants, dextromethorphan, stimulants, certain opioids), side effects like insomnia/anxiety, impulse-control issues, hallucinations, and safe discontinuation.
